design_note: Timeline supports full-war/month/week/day/hour filtering. hour_bucket remains null unless a source supports an hour. Do not fabricate hour values.

records.summary: USAFCENT publicly demonstrated distributed CAOC operations years before the 2026 war.
U.S. and Iraq jointly commit to a Higher Military Commission to determine how the coalition mission will evolve.
The U.S.-Iraq Higher Military Commission begins its working process.
Washington and Baghdad formally announce the two-phase transition timeline for the coalition military mission.
United States and Saudi Arabia sign the Strategic Defense Agreement before the Iran war.
A multinational Middle East air-defense coordination cell opened inside Al Udeid’s CAOC before the war.
Some personnel were advised to leave Al Udeid amid escalating tensions before the war.
Iraq assumes full control of Ain al-Asad after U.S. forces depart under the pre-war U.S.-Iraq transition.
USS Abraham Lincoln was already in the Arabian Sea on a scheduled deployment three weeks before the war began.
U.S. completes al-Tanf withdrawal and hands the base to Syrian government forces after U.S.-Syrian coordination.
Syrian forces take control of Shaddadi after coordination with the United States.
A senior U.S. official publicly characterizes the Syria reduction as a deliberate and conditions-based transition.
U.S. begins withdrawing from Qasrak, its main northeast Syria base, five days before the Iran war.
Pre-war nuclear talks ended with reported progress but no agreement.
A public claim about an imminent Iranian long-range missile threat was reported as unsupported by U.S. intelligence.
The United States and Israel opened major strikes on Iran; Iran retaliated regionally.
Pentagon briefing reportedly said there was no intelligence Iran planned to attack U.S. forces first.
Hormuz shipping and war-risk costs collapsed from normal conditions immediately after the opening attacks.
Qatar sought to strengthen its U.S. security partnership after Iranian strikes.
Tracked Hormuz traffic had fallen by roughly 97% from pre-war levels.
Several U.S. allies declined or avoided committing warships to a Hormuz escort effort.
A report alleged Russia was sharing satellite imagery and drone technology with Iran.
The United States accelerated additional troop and amphibious reinforcement to the Middle East.
Attacks expanded to major Iranian and Gulf energy infrastructure.
Washington threatened Iranian power plants; Iran threatened regional energy, IT and desalination targets in response.
Iran threatened mine laying and a fuller Gulf closure if coastal sites were attacked.
Iran was reviewing a U.S. 15-point proposal as the oil disruption accumulated.
The U.S. announced a temporary pause on attacks against Iranian energy plants while a ceasefire proposal was under review.
The Houthis entered the war while U.S. Marines arrived in the region.
IAEA reporting said the Khondab heavy-water facility was severely damaged and no longer operational.
One-month reporting found several stated U.S. objectives remained unresolved and Iran retained strike capacity.
WSJ-reported U.S. deliberations suggested the war might end without first restoring Hormuz.
Pakistan-mediated diplomacy produced a temporary two-week ceasefire.
The United States began a blockade aimed at vessels entering or leaving Iranian ports after talks failed.
Parties disputed who had sought the ceasefire while discussing another negotiating round.
U.S. forces seized/boarded an Iranian cargo vessel during the ceasefire period.
Iran seized two container ships after the earlier U.S. cargo seizure.
Chinese independent refiners continued buying Iranian crude despite the conflict and blockade lag.
Iran’s economy was under severe strain but had not immediately collapsed.
Washington sought international help to reopen Hormuz while Iran warned against renewed attacks.
Project Freedom began/was emphasized, but commercial shipping remained largely at a standstill.
Iranian media claimed a U.S. warship was hit by missiles and turned back.
Secretary Rubio said Operation Epic Fury had concluded and Project Freedom was a separate defensive operation.
Iran stated that most vessels could transit if they coordinated with its navy, except designated enemies.
An Iranian drone strike hit an electrical generator outside Barakah’s inner perimeter; one reactor automatically shut down.
Negotiating positions remained far apart on nuclear restrictions, blockade relief, guarantees, reparations and Hormuz.
Pakistan delivered a revised Iranian proposal; Trump said a planned U.S. attack was paused.
Iran developed a tiered passage system using checkpoints, state arrangements and selective transit approvals.
UN Security Council condemned the Barakah attack without attributing responsibility.
Negotiators reached provisional 60-day ceasefire and shipping terms, pending leadership approval, while strikes continued.
Fresh strike claims and U.S. sanctions on the Persian Gulf Strait Authority showed the conflict remained active.
Iran sought a limited interim deal to relieve economic pressure and buy negotiating time.
An Iranian drone/missile attack damaged Kuwait International Airport and killed one person.
U.S. officials said an interim memorandum had been signed and Hormuz traffic would be restored gradually.
The 14-point interim U.S.-Iran framework was published/reported in detail.
Israel and Lebanon sign a U.S.-mediated security framework in Washington.
Industry reporting quantified major LNG trade loss from the Hormuz disruption.
The June interim arrangement was publicly treated as over after renewed attacks.
Iran reported attacks on U.S. military infrastructure across Gulf states and Jordan; U.S. forces reported a large strike response.
IRGC Navy publicly declared the Strait closed until further notice.
Houthis declared a naval blockade against Saudi Arabia.
Saudi Arabia unveils a proposed multinational maritime-defense coalition backed by a 14-state joint statement.
A new Hormuz proposal exposed unresolved differences over inspections, fees and control.
Saudi Arabia, Türkiye and Pakistan sign the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement.
Pakistan made a final mediation push before the 60-day negotiating window expired.
U.S.-mediated talks consider four countries as possible contributors to a Hezbollah disarmament verification mechanism.

records.time: Physical movement began approximately late July; exact day unresolved
records.summary: AP reports the Erbil drawdown is underway under the pre-war 2024 U.S.-Iraq transition; Sept. 30, 2026 remains the planned endpoint.
records.physical_event_time_text: Late July 2026 (approximate; AP Aug. 12 said about three weeks earlier)

records.summary: The U.S. said it could sustain the naval blockade indefinitely by rotating forces as oil-supply shortfalls deepened.
Two ADNOC vessels were attacked; the UAE blamed Iran, which had not accepted responsibility at publication.
Lebanon denies that a final four-country verification shortlist has been agreed; talks with the United States continue.
Hormuz traffic remained capped at a small fraction of pre-war levels.
The Navy announced Lincoln would return home as part of a planned rotation after an extended combat deployment.
Tracked commodity-vessel traffic fell to five Saturday and zero Sunday at Reuters’ snapshot after tanker attacks.
The 60-day negotiating window expired without a final deal; Iran threatened a more offensive Hormuz posture.
Iranian inflation and food-price pressure had reached extreme levels.
Washington said the Strait was open and no talks were under way; Tehran said it remained shut pending compliance with June terms.
Chinese state shippers increasingly avoided Hormuz/Bab el-Mandeb and used tanker positioning/ship-to-ship transfers outside the Gulf.
The UAE halted financial/economic dealings with Iran after alleging Iranian ballistic missiles targeted maritime traffic.
Interested Allied states coordinate possible national freedom-of-navigation contributions for Hormuz; this is not a NATO mission.
Hormuz tracked commodity-vessel traffic was unchanged at nine Tuesday and nine Wednesday; Bab el-Mandeb fell to 27 Wednesday from 32 Tuesday.
Washington announced a new escalation of economic pressure on Iran and threatened consequences for countries providing a lifeline.
USS George Washington arrived to relieve USS Abraham Lincoln while another U.S. carrier remained in theater.
Oil prices remained elevated as markets assessed war and negotiation risk.
Iran’s central bank governor said oil exports had fallen to zero and foreign-exchange access was severely constrained.
Kpler/Reuters records seven Aug. 20 commodity-vessel transits; no VLCC or LNG tanker in the observed seven.
Later Reuters reporting gives a four-commodity-ship observation for the same Thursday period; discrepancy remains unresolved.
U.S. blockade pressure sharply reduces Iranian crude availability to Chinese buyers while market adaptation continues.
Qalibaf advocates deeper Iran-Iraq economic ties and national-currency trade to reduce sanctions/dollar exposure.
Iraq pursues higher production and multiple export-route hedges, including Ceyhan and proposed Baniyas/Aqaba options.
Oman and Iran discuss suitable conditions for renewed dialogue and continued practical Hormuz navigation understandings.
Two U.S. KC-135 tanker aircraft depart Bezmer after a temporary, pre-authorized deployment; causation by Iranian pressure is not established.
World Bank says renewed conflict derailed Lebanon’s fragile recovery, projecting 2026 contraction and high inflation.
Pezeshkian says the war should end now while framing termination as compatible with Iranian strength, dignity and victory.
Iran grants special Hormuz passage permission to some Iraqi oil tankers after repeated Iraqi requests.
France and Saudi Arabia discuss Hormuz alternatives and an energy/logistics task-force track.
Iranian Armed Forces chief threatens severe retaliation and authorities claim improved missile-production quantity/quality.
Qalibaf says Iran received numerous messages from neighboring states about regional security/economic arrangements; counterparties are unidentified.
U.S. says details of a severe new Iran sanctions package are scheduled for Aug. 24; measures are not yet enacted at cutoff.
